summary: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and retrieving the minimum in O(1).
mainInsight: The minimum of a stack only changes when elements are pushed or popped, so remember 'the minimum so far' alongside every element: pushing computes min(previous min, new value), popping simply discards the top of both.

approaches.name: Parallel min stack
approaches.summary: A second stack stores the running minimum for each position.

approaches.name: Push only new minimums
approaches.summary: Second stack only gets a value when it is <= the current min.
strengths: Saves memory when mins are rare

personalSolution.notes: Optimal in time. The 'push only new minimums' variant saves memory.

options: Store the running minimum alongside each element
Keep the whole stack sorted after every single push

cards.answer: Store the running minimum alongside each element
cards.explanation: Each state of the stack has a fixed minimum, so recording it per position gives O(1) retrieval after any pop.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Use a heap for all elements instead of a: Heap operations are O(log n) and removal of arbitrary elements is awkward.

promptVariants: Why does popping not require recomputing the minimum?
Why is a per-position running minimum sufficient?
cards.answer: When an element is popped, the stack returns exactly to an earlier state, and the minimum recorded at that earlier state is the correct one. So each push stores min(prev_min, value) and each pop simply discards the top of both stacks.
keyPoints: Stack states are restored on pop

promptVariants: What is the invariant between `stack` and `mins` in your solution?
How do the two stacks stay in sync?
cards.answer: They always have the same length, and mins[i] equals the minimum of stack[0..i]. Every push appends to both; every pop removes from both.

What is the space cost and how can it be reduced?
How would you reduce the memory of the second stack?
cards.answer: O(n) for the extra stack. You can push onto mins only when the new value is <= the current minimum (and pop it only when the popped value equals it), saving memory when new minimums are rare.
cards.explanation: Using < would break with duplicate minimums.

promptVariants: Why does push use min(self.mins[-1], value) and why must pop remove from both stacks?
What would break if pop forgot the mins stack?
cards.answer: The new minimum is either the old minimum or the new value. Pop must remove both entries so the stacks stay aligned; otherwise getMin would return a stale minimum belonging to an element that is no longer in the stack.
keyPoints: min of old min and new value
cards.explanation: The `if not self.stack: return` guard hides invalid calls; the problem guarantees non-empty stacks.
